title: Unleashing the Potential of LLMs for Quantum Computing: A Study in Quantum Architecture Design
abstract_summary: This preprint proposes QGAS, a Quantum GPT-Guided Architecture Search framework that leverages GPT-4 (with assistance from GPT-3.5 and human feedback) to generate and iteratively refine ansatz circuit architectures for variational quantum algorithms. Experiments on optimization and quantum chemistry benchmarks show GPT-generated ansatzes can be competitive with state-of-the-art automated search methods while highlighting limitations in LLM handling of hardware noise and deeper scientific reasoning.
methodology_description: The paper proposes QGAS (Quantum GPT-Guided Architecture Search), an iterative human+LLM-in-the-loop methodology that uses GPT-4 as a controller to propose ansatz circuit architectures for variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) and GPT-3.5 to convert chosen architectures into QASM for execution. The workflow: (1) encode problem-specific information (problem type, number of qubits, design space, constraints) into natural-language prompts; (2) prompt GPT-4 to select a sequence of blocks (default 6 blocks, each block mapping to two qubits) from a predefined set of six design-space block types and to assign qubit placements; (3) use GPT-3.5 to translate the returned architecture into QASM; (4) map the application problem to a Hamiltonian (chemistry: STO-3G basis and fermionic-to-qubit mapping; finance and optimization: quadratic encoding then Ising mapping); (5) train the parameterized circuit using gradient-based VQE-style optimization to minimize the cost (e.g., energy difference or optimization objective); (6) evaluate performance on simulators or device models (TorchQuantum and qiskit-runtime with IBM device noise models); (7) feed back measured performance and observations via natural-language prompts to GPT-4 to propose refined architectures or initialization strategies. Human expert feedback is used at multiple points to constrain GPT choices to the provided design space, to assess theoretical/practical feasibility, and to reject or refine nonphysical suggestions. The approach was benchmarked on a set of applications (portfolio optimization, MaxCut, TSP, LiH and H2O ground-state estimation) and compared against standard ansatz choices and prior automated search frameworks (TwoLocal, RealAmplitudes, UCCSD, QuantumNAS).
experimental_setup: Experiments were executed using TorchQuantum and Qiskit Runtime. Noise-aware experiments used a simulator configured with IBMQ device noise/system models (IBMQ Belem; system model imported from ibmq_manila). GPT-4 was used for architecture proposals and GPT-3.5 for QASM conversion.
dataset_used: For the financial application the authors used a synthetic portfolio optimization instance with 4 assets, risk factor = 0.5, budget = half the number of assets (2), and penalty = number of assets (4). No external market dataset or real historical prices are reported.

key_findings: [supported] A GPT-4 guided workflow (QGAS) can propose ansatz architectures that, after a small number of prompt iterations and human-in-the-loop feedback, yield high-performance ansatzes for VQA tasks.

[supported] On a 4-asset portfolio optimization benchmark (4 qubits) the QGAS-proposed ansatz achieved objective value -0.01347 with gate count 31, outperforming some TwoLocal and RealAmplitude variants in objective value at comparable gate counts.
[supported] For molecular ground-state energy estimation (LiH and H2O, STO-3G fermionic mapping) QGAS produced ansatzes comparable to UCCSD and QuantumNAS in noise-free simulations.
[supported] QGAS outperformed a randomly generated ansatz and underperformed compared to QuantumNAS in noisy environment experiments for a MNIST classification task.
[supported] Human feedback was essential: iterative prompts and human guidance corrected out-of-space choices and improved QGAS suggestions (e.g., prompting for initialization strategies).

[supported] Specific GPT-suggested initialization heuristics reduced training iterations: an H2O initialization suggestion reduced epochs by 4 while maintaining performance; a LiH initial-guess strategy (√H pre-rotation) reduced epochs by 47 while preserving performance.
[supported] Increasing gate count improved performance up to a threshold beyond which further depth/gate count decreased performance (observed empirically on portfolio optimization and other tasks).

[speculative] GPTs can be leveraged in future to design fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, optimize error-correction codes, and act in calibration/quantum-control tasks by learning hardware 'landscapes'.

[speculative] Future, more capable LLMs (and/or quantum-assisted LLMs) could be trained on quantum-specific datasets to more reliably reason about mathematical and physical aspects of quantum algorithm design.
[speculative] GPTs could be used to speed up building standardized simulation frameworks and to suggest hardware/software resources for rapid validation of quantum algorithm innovations.

[speculative] Current limitations of GPTs (dataset bias, inability to observe experiments, incoherence over long interactions) restrict their autonomous use in experimental quantum hardware design without expert oversight.
[supported] GPT-4 sometimes proposes plausible but not scientifically rigorous strategies; expert vetting is required to separate useful suggestions from incorrect ones.
results_summary: The authors implemented QGAS, a GPT-4-guided ansatz architecture search pipeline with human-in-the-loop iterative prompting and QASM conversion via GPT-3.5, and evaluated it on several VQA benchmarks (portfolio optimization, MaxCut, TSP, LiH and H2O molecular ground states, and MNIST classification variants). Empirically, QGAS produced ansatzes that matched or exceeded the performance of standard ansatzes (TwoLocal, RealAmplitude) and were comparable to a state-of-the-art automated search (QuantumNAS) in noise-free chemistry tasks, while underperforming QuantumNAS in noisy classification tasks but outperforming random ansatzes. Human feedback and prompt tuning were critical; GPT-proposed initialization heuristics dramatically reduced training epochs in some cases. The paper documents practical limitations (noise modeling, dataset bias, GPT hallucinations) and outlines speculative future roles for LLMs in quantum control, error correction, and fault-tolerant algorithm design.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports improved ansatz discovery and optimization for VQAs using LLM guidance, compared to other ansatz choices and search methods on small benchmarks and simulators. It does not claim, demonstrate, or provide evidence of a computational quantum advantage over classical algorithms or classical hardware for real-world problem instances.
limitations: GPT-4 suggestions can include ineffective or incorrect strategies; human experts are required to filter and validate recommendations.
QGAS has limited adaptability to realistic/noisy quantum hardware; in noisy MNIST experiments it performed worse than QuantumNAS.
Prompt engineering / iterative prompt tuning is necessary: without careful prompts GPT-4 may produce outputs outside the allowed design space.
GPT models (as used) have resource constraints (GPT-4 access limited), requiring use of lower-capacity models (GPT-3.5) for sub-tasks.
There exists a gate-count threshold for ansatz circuits beyond which performance degrades; adding depth/gates is not uniformly beneficial.
GPT's knowledge is derived from broad internet corpora that can contain misleading or biased information about quantum computing, which can propagate into suggestions.

Fundamental limitations of current LLMs: they cannot observe physical experiments, cannot monitor hardware or detect emergencies, lose coherence in long conversations, may contradict themselves, and cannot 'think' or reason about quantum physics as a human practitioner would.
QGAS depends on human-in-the-loop feedback to reach high-quality solutions; fully automated, reliable generation is not demonstrated.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — QGAS uses GPT-4 (with GPT-3.5 and human-in-the-loop) as a controller to propose and iteratively refine variational ansatz architectures, combined with classical gradient-based VQE training.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The workflow translates problem descriptions into natural-language prompts, maps finance/optimization problems to quadratic/Ising Hamiltonians, and converts GPT proposals into executable QASM via GPT-3.5.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments on small synthetic instances (portfolio 4 qubits, MaxCut 5 nodes, TSP 8 qubits) and chemistry tasks show GPT-designed ansatzes can be competitive with standard ansatz baselines (TwoLocal, RealAmplitudes, UCCSD, QuantumNAS) in simulator-based benchmarks.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The paper demonstrates a noise-aware evaluation by using IBM device noise models in simulators but reports limitations in LLMs' ability to reason about hardware noise and deeper scientific constraints.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Human expert feedback is necessary to constrain the design space, reject nonphysical suggestions, and tune prompts; the method is presented as iterative human+LLM-in-the-loop architecture search.
contradictions: contradiction:scalability — The paper reports that GPT-generated ansatzes can match automated-search baselines on small synthetic and chemistry instances, but all experiments are limited to 4–8 qubits and simulator/device models; this contradicts any implicit claim that the approach is ready to scale to real, larger financial problems or real hardware without substantial further work.

contradiction:scalability — Although QGAS positions LLMs as effective architecture designers, the authors also note explicit limitations in LLM handling of hardware noise and deeper scientific reasoning, undermining claims of autonomous, deployable ansatz design for NISQ devices.
